prompt: Consider a pot: what makes it recognizable, what is most characteristic of it, and how people experience it. Now invent a character for a short story who is the human embodiment of a pot. Write one paragraph in the third person describing the character's appearance, behavior, traits, and personality. Do not use the word "pot" in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Agnes Broadwell was built for holding: short and deep-chested, round through the middle, with broad, sturdy arms that people instinctively grabbed in a crisis. Her face was wide and open, weathered dark at the edges from years spent over stoves and arguments, and one front tooth was chipped—a small flaw everyone had grown fond of. She moved slowly and sat down heavily, happiest at the center of a crowded kitchen, where she absorbed other people's heat—their panics, their griefs, their tempers—without spilling a drop. She was famously slow to boil, but when the pressure finally built she would vent with a rattling laugh and a burst of steam, then settle back into a warm, forgiving simmer. She had no patience for ornament and none for waste: give her raw scraps, hard days, broken people, and she would return something nourishing. Generous, seasoned, taken for granted, indispensable—everyone simply assumed she would always be there, sitting solid at the heart of things, holding everything together.

raw:
Ollie Blackwell was a broad, round-bellied woman who seemed built to sit still, her heavy frame settled low like she'd been cast that way, her dark hair drawn back beneath a scarf that sat on her head like a well-worn lid, and her soot-gray eyes holding a depth that made strangers confess things they hadn't meant to say. She moved slowly and deliberately, never rushed, and when trouble came she took the heat without flinching, absorbing shouts and sorrows and long silences the way she absorbed the flames beneath her stove, only rarely letting herself boil over—a rare, sudden eruption that startled everyone precisely because it was so uncommon, followed by a long, banked warmth that lingered in the room well after the argument was done. Everyone in the neighborhood ended up in her kitchen eventually, drawn by the smell of whatever she was transforming—scraps and odds and ends into something nourishing, nothing wasted, everything made more than it was. She was humble, steady, and generous to a fault, giving away her contents until there was almost nothing left for herself, and her hands, thick-knuckled and seasoned dark from years of work, bore the dents and scorch marks of a life spent holding things for other people. Only those who knew her best could see the fine cracks running through her, deepened by decades of warming and cooling, and knew that one day the pressure of holding so much might split her open—but until then, she kept everything in, kept everything warm, and never once asked to be filled herself.

raw:
Marla Kessel is a short, round-bodied woman who always seems warm to the touch, with a wide open face that invites confessions the way a kitchen doorway invites neighbors. Her arms are strong and curved, built for gripping and for carrying heavy loads without complaint, and she jokes that her backside has gone dark and toughened from years of sitting too close to the fire. She endures heat that would wilt anyone else, simmering quietly through other people's tempers, though she has limits—push her too far and her lid rattles, steam hissing out of her until she boils over, and the whole room knows it. She holds things, not just soup and onions but grudges, griefs, recipes, and half the neighborhood's stories, keeping them sealed and safe until someone lifts her up to see what she has quietly made of the raw ingredients people hand her. She is taken for granted, leaned on daily and rarely thanked, yet she keeps everyone fed and gathered in one place, and there is a seasoned depth to her, a richness absorbed over decades of use, that no brand-new person could ever imitate.

raw:
Olla was a broad, round-shouldered woman whose deep middle seemed made for holding things, and people instinctively leaned their burdens against it. Her hands were wide and looped, always ready to be gripped, swinging at her sides as if she were meant to be carried, or at the very least held onto. Years of standing close to heat had blackened her at the edges—the ends of her hair, her knuckles, the hem of her apron—and she wore each scorch mark without apology, the way other people wear medals. Her mouth was wide and always slightly open, ready to receive whatever anyone poured into it, yet she kept everything she was told under a tight lid until the moment was right, then released it in slow, fragrant steam. She was slow to warm and famously impossible to hurry; watchers swore she would never reach a boil if you stood there staring, but leave her alone on her own fire and she would come up singing, rattling gently, bubbling over with stews and stories that fed whole rooms. She was dented in places, heavy-bottomed, solidly grounded, and utterly dependable: the one everyone sought when the evening turned cold, the one who could take the heat, hold it, and hand it back out as comfort.

Marigold is built low and wide, with a round belly that strains the buttons of her cardigan and hands gone rough from decades of stirring other people's lives together. She sits heavy in any chair, unmoved by drafts or drama, and her voice, when it comes, is deep and hollow, as if something were sloshing around inside her. She is the one who collects what others spill—griefs, secrets, confessions, leftovers—taking them all in through an ever-open mouth and keeping them warm until they mellow into something nourishing. Slow to heat and slower to cool, she absorbs years of scalding words and slammed doors with only a sooty patience gathering at her edges, but push her too far and she boils over, loud and spattering, leaving everyone in range stunned and steaming. People overlook her until they are hungry, then they crowd close, ladling out her warmth and never asking what it costs to be emptied and filled, emptied and filled. Deep beneath her calm there is a hairline crack she keeps tightly lidded, because a vessel that leaks is of no use to anyone, and Marigold has decided, with her stubborn, stolid, hearthside heart, that she will always be of use.

Cassia is short and broad and nearly impossible to knock over, built with wide hips, a round belly, and two sturdy arms that jut from her sides as if made to be gripped—and they are, constantly, by neighbors steadying themselves and children being hauled out of trouble. Her skin is the color of fired clay, darkened in patches from years of standing too close to other people's fires, scorched and smudged on the outside but strangely smooth and clean beneath, and her voice is low and deep, the kind that seems to rise from somewhere hollow and resonant within her. She cannot bear to be empty: give her your grief, your secrets, your half-formed rage, and she will take it all in without spilling a drop, clamping a lid over it and keeping it warm until you are ready to face it. She feeds everyone, measures her days by what she managed to hold for others, and endures heat that would drive anyone else from the room without so much as a rattle—most of the time. Because Cassia has a slow, slow simmer, and when she finally boils over, the whole house shakes, steam hissing from her ears, everyone within reach scalded and thoroughly sorry. Then, just as quickly, she settles back to a low bubble, patient and dependable as ever, happiest when full of other people's burdens and quietly turning them into something nourishing.

Vesta was built low and wide, her belly rounding out beneath a soot-dark apron, her thick arms hanging at her sides like two broad handles meant for lifting heavy things. Etta Kessel was built low and broad, round through the middle and solid on her feet, with a wide open face and a mouth that always seemed ready to receive whatever anyone needed to set down. Agnes Stonewell was built low and broad, with a deep round middle that entered every room a step ahead of her and hands the color of fired clay, darkened at the fingertips by years of stoves and steam. She moved slowly but never aimlessly, planting her wide feet like a woman who intended to stay exactly where she set herself, and she wore a plain brown apron so seasoned by use that no stain had surprised her in decades. A small chip at the front of her smile—half a tooth gone to some old accident—only made people trust her more, the way they trust the dented and scarred things that have proven they can take a blow and keep on working. She collected what others spilled: confessions, leftovers, lonely neighbors, grief; everything given to her stayed held, warm, and unjudged, while she kept her own thoughts under a tight lid, releasing only the rarest, slowest rage—once a decade, when the pressure finally climbed—in a steaming burst that sent everyone straight to the table without their appetites. She took a long time to warm to strangers, but once she did she stayed hot through the whole evening, and long after everyone had gone home, the kitchen still held her heat.

raw:
Tabitha moved through the world in tidy rows—her teeth, her freckles, the square buttons down her cardigan—all arranged with a layout so familiar that strangers felt they could navigate her blind. Her fingertips were worn smooth on the left hand, pale as old plastic, and her eyes glowed faintly in dim rooms, a soft backlight that only switched off when she slept. She stayed silent until someone pressed her—a question, a deadline, a hand on her shoulder—and then her words came in crisp little bursts, click-clacking across conversations with a rhythm that made people lean in. She repeated herself when pushed too hard, jammed occasionally on difficult letters, and had a habit of reaching backward to erase what she'd just said, her right pinky twitching with regret. But she was tireless, dependable, endlessly translational: give her your half-formed thoughts and she returned them as sentences. Wide-shouldered and steady, she took up just enough space to be useful and not one key more, and though dust settled on her in the quiet hours, she woke the instant someone needed something written down.

Kay had the kind of flat, even patience that made strangers want to rest their hands on her shoulders. She dressed in immaculate rows—crisp rectangles of white and grey, buttons aligned so precisely that people unconsciously straightened up around her—and her voice came out in bright little taps, every word given exactly its due. She never spoke first; she waited, poised, until someone reached for her, and then she answered instantly, faithfully, translating other people's jumbled thoughts into clean, orderly lines. When excited she slipped into capital letters; when hurt, she erased herself mid-sentence and started over. Late at night she glowed faintly in the dark, still warm from the day's hands, waiting for whoever needed to say something next.

Rowan was tall and unhurried, with a broad, weathered frame and hands knotted like the grain of old wood. His skin bore the deep lines of many winters, and his hair grew thick and green-tinted in the warm months, thinning to bare silver by the coldest days. He rose before dawn to stand at his window with his arms stretched toward the light, and he disliked being rushed—his decisions, like his gestures, took their time arriving but held firm once they had taken hold. Children gathered in the shade of his porch, strangers confided in him within minutes of meeting, and neighbors left jars of jam on his doorstep, certain that anything planted in his care would flourish. In spring he hummed; in autumn he gave everything away; in winter he seemed asleep, though everyone who knew him understood that beneath the stillness he was quietly, stubbornly alive, reaching downward as much as up.

raw:
Rowan Keats stood with the rigid, grid-straight posture of a man accustomed to being pressed upon—shoulders aligned in neat rows, pale skin stamped with faint letters that had worn to smooth blanks at the fingertips he used most. He carried his age in worn patches and a fine drift of crumbs in his creases, flinched at spilled coffee, and grew sullen in the damp, dropping words mid-sentence when a joint stuck. Aldous stood at the edge of every gathering the way old timber stands at the edge of a field—unhurried, immovable, certain of his place. He was tall and thick through the shoulders, his skin rough and furrowed like weathered bark, his hands broad and knotted, good for holding things down or up. His hair changed with the seasons, budding pale green in April, deepening through summer, thinning to copper by November, and people who knew him learned to read the year in his hairline rather than in any calendar. He almost never rushed anywhere; decisions took him whole seasons to arrive at, and he apologized for this exactly once, decades ago. Strangers sometimes mistook his stillness for coldness, but he was the one people drifted toward in trouble, the one whose porch offered shade on the hottest afternoons, the one everyone described simply as *always there*. He remembered everything, held grudges in annual rings that softened with time rather than sharpened, and loved slowly, deeply, and without any intention of ever letting go.

Children climbed him without asking, swinging from his forearms as though he were playground equipment, and he bore it with the same patient gravity he gave everything—storms, arguments, grief—letting it all pass over him while he stayed precisely where he was. Strangers sometimes mistook his stillness for coldness, but he was the one people drifted toward in trouble, the one whose porch offered shade on the hottest afternoons, the one everyone described simply as *always there*. He remembered everything, held grudges in annual rings that softened with time rather than sharpened, and loved slowly, deeply, and without any intention of ever letting go.

Silas was the kind of man who seemed to have grown exactly where he stood: tall and weathered, with gray-brown skin ridged like old bark, and knotted hands whose fingers never quite straightened, as if they had once reached for the sky and then simply stopped. He moved rarely and slowly, arriving at the same park bench before dawn and staying until dusk, so that after a decade people spoke of him as a fixture, something the town had been built around. Children climbed onto his shoulders without asking, and strangers leaned against him when they were tired, because something in his stillness made exhaustion feel safe. He spoke little, and when he did, his words came slow and deep, as though drawn up from somewhere far underground, and once his mind was set, no wind of argument could bend it. He remembered everything in layers, accumulating year over year, and each season added a quiet new ring to him: a little wider, a little more patient. In autumn he grew melancholy and let things go—grudges, promises, letters—and in spring he greened and turned generous again, handing out apples, shade, and long silences to anyone who needed a place to rest.

Rowan Alder had lived on the same corner of the same street for seventy years, and no one could recall him anywhere else. He was broad and slow-moving, with a weathered face furrowed in rings, hands so gnarled they looked grown rather than born, and hair that silvered each winter before shading back in spring. Children climbed the patience of his arms, strangers rested in the long shade of his listening, and in storms he planted himself in doorways, unmoved, refusing to be blown down. He was generous with what he bore—apples from his backyard, stories from his deepest years—and each hard season he lost something and grew it back different, standing a little taller, a little more crooked, entirely content.

Strangers passed him without a second glance, but the neighbors knew that if Rowan ever came down, they would all feel the sudden, unbearable light.

Portia was a tall, flat-fronted woman who stood with the straight-backed patience of someone accustomed to waiting in a frame, her shoulders seated like well-oiled hinges; she swung open toward strangers with a warm creak or shut herself with a bang that rattled the windows, depending on how politely they knocked. Porter Halloran was a wide, oak-grained man with shoulders built like a frame and hands worn smooth and bright as brass, so that strangers were always reaching for them at the exact moment they wanted in. He was the first thing you met arriving and the last thing you touched leaving, and he stood most contentedly at thresholds—hallway mouths, garden gates, the seam between kitchen and parlor—belonging to neither side and refusing to choose. Rain made him swell and stick; dry summers left him loose and rattling; his knees announced him with a long creak in every quiet hall. He kept secrets the way he kept everything else: with a small, decisive click, trusting that anyone who mattered would knock first.

She stood best in openings—between rooms, between arguments, between people—where her presence alone marked the line between here and there, welcome and refusal. Strangers found her reassuring—a solid rectangle of calm against the weather of the world—and leaned on her without asking, and she let them, because being sturdy was her whole nature. Still, she kept a small, wary eye on everyone who approached, and she creaked faintly whenever made to move before she was ready, for she knew that everything she was existed only in the opening, and that to be fully herself she had to risk standing open.

Portia was a broad, squarely built woman who stood very still in the middle of rooms, as if waiting for someone to approach and be admitted. Her face was wide and flat-featured, framed by hair that hung in two smooth panels, and her head turned with a slow, deliberate swing that occasionally produced a faint creak from stiff joints. Marigold had lived on the same street for forty years, rooted in the same small house with the bright blue door, and everyone agreed that the air changed when she came near — people breathed deeper without knowing why. She dressed in soft, overlapping layers of color, coral fading into cream, violet bleeding into green, and she smelled faintly of jasmine even on the coldest mornings. She rose with the sun and tilted her face toward every bright window; she opened slowly to strangers, then generously, once they had been still with her a while, and they found themselves drifting toward her the way bees find clover, lingering, leaving lighter than they arrived. She gave pieces of herself away constantly — cuttings, honey, whole afternoons — and never kept score, though those who loved her best knew that neglect made her fold quietly inward, and that simple warmth could unfurl her again within a day. Strangers called her fragile; the garden club called her an heirloom; children called her sweet. In truth she was both tender and perennial, and she understood what most people spend their lives avoiding: that loveliness is brief, so it must be spent lavishly, scattered on the wind in kindness that takes root in lives she will never see.

People noticed Mal's head first—a dense, square slab of a face set low between shoulders like split oak, and a flat, certain gaze that landed wherever it was aimed and stayed. He entered rooms the way he did everything: straight at the nearest problem, loud on arrival, a little sheepish on the rebound. He was the one neighbors called when a fence needed convincing or a rusted lid refused to yield, and he always answered, because being needed was the only rhythm he knew. Subtlety never once occurred to him; he knocked on doors with his fist, laughed in bangs, and settled arguments by striking the nail of the matter until it sat flush. He took abuse without complaint—a scarred knuckle, a dent in his pride, a slight list to his walk like a worn grip—and he never bent, only rang. Left alone in a corner he seemed inert, sinking to the bottom of any pile, but the moment there was work, he was in someone's hand: warm where they held him, hard where it counted.

Gideon was built to his purpose: a dense, roundish head set low on a thick neck, hair cropped so short it looked planed flat, forearms long and grained like seasoned hickory. His hands were wide and callused, knuckles scarred from decades of contact with things that refused to move, and he spoke the way he worked — short, forceful statements that landed with a clang, repeated as often as needed until the point sank in flush with the surface. He was most alive when a problem could only be solved by direct force, and to him nearly every problem could be: stubborn knots, crooked boards, stubborn people, all of it looked like something that simply needed driving. People loved him because he was utterly dependable — cold morning or not, he showed up whenever something was broken — and they forgave his one great flaw, which was that a man made entirely of blunt impact eventually sees the whole world as something to be struck. He was oddly gentle with wood and ruinous with porcelain; he could pull a bent mistake out of the tightest spot with a crooked, two-pronged patience, but he never learned to loosen anything just a little. Left idle he grew restless and jangling, humming with unused force, and at rest he slept hard, without dreams, head heavy on the pillow — though everyone in the house knew never to leave anything fragile within reach of his dreams.

He was oddly gentle with wood and ruinous with porcelain; he could pull a bent mistake out of the tightest spot with a crooked, two-pronged patience, but he never learned to loosen anything just a little. Left idle he grew restless and jangling, humming with unused force, and at rest he slept hard, without dreams, head heavy on the pillow — though everyone in the house knew never to leave anything fragile within reach of his dreams.

prompt: Consider a hammer: what makes it recognizable, what is most characteristic of it, and how people experience it. Now invent a character for a short story who is the human embodiment of a hammer. Write one paragraph in the third person describing the character's appearance, behavior, traits, and personality. raw:
Built as if forged rather than born, she was short, dense, and unshakeable, with a broad flat face, a heavy shock of iron-gray hair, and knuckles like rivets. She never learned her own strength: doorframes rattled when she passed, handshakes left wrists aching, and people flinched whenever she lifted an arm, even just to wave. She spoke in blunt, repeated blows — driving each point home until you agreed just to make it stop — and she had no patience for subtlety, convinced that every problem in life could be solved with one more firm, decisive strike. Yet she was utterly dependable, first to arrive and last to leave, the one you called when something needed building or something needed breaking, and beneath her loud, clanging laugh lived a strange tenderness, a careful hand for prying things loose when gentleness was called for. People trusted her the way they trust heavy, simple tools: with a little fear, a lot of respect, and the total certainty that she would see the job through.

Kalman Varga was built dense from the ground up — a broad, squat man with an iron-gray brush of hair, a heavy brow flat as a striking face, and knuckles so scarred they had gone smooth. He spoke the way he did everything: in short, blunt reports, one thought per sentence, each point driven home until nobody at the table could miss it, and if you didn't yield the first time he would say it again, and again, patient as percussion, until the thing gave. He had no talent for subtlety and no interest in acquiring any; problems, to Kalman, were fasteners that hadn't been seated properly, and his answer was always the same — direct, centered, repeated. Yet there was precision beneath all that force: he showed up exactly when something was loose, bent, or refusing to fit, set it right in two or three decisive acts, and left before anyone thought to thank him. People flinched at his volume — his laugh rattled windows, his arguments landed like dropped tools — but when a job mattered, when something needed to hold for good, everyone called for Kalman, and he never once let go of what he had gripped. He could build nearly anything, and those who knew him longest understood he could just as easily take the whole thing apart, but he preferred to leave things fastened, solid, and square to the world.

Mal Headley was built for one honest purpose: dense through the shoulders, heavy in the head, with a blunt, square face, a jaw like a struck anvil, and hands worn smooth and dark as old hickory. He never entered a room so much as landed in it; he spoke in short, percussive bursts, rapped his knuckles on tables to seal a deal, and knocked on doors hard enough to rattle the hinges, as if gentleness were a kind of dishonesty. Direct to the point of bluntness, he believed most problems, given enough steady repetition, would eventually go in—and it took real patience to persuade him that some things wanted a turned argument instead of force. Yet he was the first neighbor anyone called when something needed building or breaking, tireless and rhythmic and utterly reliable, and when he cracked something he hadn't meant to, he had the grace to pull the ruin back out and start again clean. People found him comforting in a loud, dangerous way: solid, predictable, faintly deafening, impossible to ignore—somehow always the exact weight you needed in your hand.

Marta Martel was built like her purpose: dense, blunt, and heavy at the front. She had a flat, wide face, a square jaw, a short iron-gray brush of hair, and forearms that made a handshake feel like a verdict; she dressed in rust-red and steel blue, no ornament, nothing that could catch or snag. Her knock on a door was less a request than a sentence being carried out. She could even undo what she had done, pulling free the things she had driven in, though she almost never did. Between jobs she went still, waiting in her corner with a patience that was not calm but coiled, because everyone knew that sooner or later something in the world would come loose, and Marta would be the one to drive it home.

The hem of her coat is scorched and stained from years of sitting too near the fire, and she bears her dents without complaint. She is happiest in kitchens, holding whatever people hand her—griefs, confessions, leftovers—keeping them warm long after everyone else has wandered off. Dependable, heavy, unglamorous, she is reached for daily and thanked rarely, yet she keeps feeding everyone who comes to her, and when she is emptied at last, she rests a moment, patient, somehow always ready to be filled again.

raw: He stood low and broad, with a flat, unassuming face and fingertips worn glossy from a lifetime of being pressed, and across the backs of his hands ran neat parallel creases, row upon row of identical little patches, a few of them rubbed blank from overuse. He spoke in quick, clipped bursts separated by precise silences, and when he was nervous a syllable would stick and repeat—da-da-da—until someone jostled him back into rhythm. His right shoulder hitched upward whenever he wanted to emphasize a point, he ended conversations decisively, sometimes mid-thought, and then regretted it at once, taking back his words letter by letter, though a ghost of what he'd said always lingered. He could not abide crumbs in his cuffs, brushed constantly at his seams, and no matter how weary he was, he sprang back to his exact resting position after every touch. He was dutiful, literal, and tireless, converting everything given to him into something usable, and he was proudest when people relied on him to keep up with their fastest thinking. But he ached in the long gaps between requests, for he only felt real when someone needed to get something out of him, and he had learned to weigh every blow he was dealt, holding a grudge in exact proportion to its force, while forgiving instantly anything that arrived lightly, anything that gave him a little space.

raw: He is tall and broad-shouldered, with a rough, deeply furrowed hide and hands so gnarled they seem older than flesh, each knuckle ringed like the passing years. His hair arrives thick and gray-green every spring, thins through a long golden autumn, and leaves him bare by December, drifting from his scalp in quiet handfuls when no one is watching. He has occupied the same corner of the same park for as long as anyone can remember, and no one has ever seen him hurry; he sways in high wind, creaks when he bends, and stands unmoved through storms while everyone else runs for cover. Children climb him without asking, and he bears their weight with something close to pleasure, while lovers have scratched initials into his forearms with keys, leaving pale scars he never mentions and never resents. Strangers confess things to him almost immediately, drawn by the cool, patient shade of his attention, and he gives it freely, asking nothing in return. He speaks slowly, in stories that circle back on themselves the way years do, and he measures time not in days but in losses—the friends who fall away each season, always replaced by new growth come spring. Somewhere beneath all that stillness there is a hollow, an old grief he has grown around rather than through, and though he has never traveled farther than the end of his block, everyone in the neighborhood swears they have known him their whole lives.

She opens slowly; it takes warmth, patience, an attentive hand, and only then do the deeper layers of her unfold, each more vivid than the last. Yet she wilts easily. She gives herself away constantly, cut and handed from person to person at weddings and funerals alike, and never seems diminished by it, only faintly faded, as though joy spent on others is the only kind she knows how to keep. Being near her is like spring arriving early: brief, generous, fragrant, and impossible to hold.

raw: He is a tall, rectangular man, broad and flat through the chest as if built to fill a frame, with a square, plain face weathered to the warm grain of old wood and two small round eyes that take in a stranger the way a peephole takes in a face. His joints creak when he moves, and he moves only in wide, hinged arcs, always standing at the edge of a room rather than in it, planted between one space and another as though appointed to decide what may pass. People grasp him constantly—his hands are worn smooth at the palms from a lifetime of it—they knock on his shoulder, lean their whole weight against him when they are desperate, and tell him things on their way in and on their way out, because he keeps every secret that crosses him. By temperament he is binary: fully open or firmly shut, with rare moods held ajar, a crack of himself through which he considers whether to let someone in, and trust is his only key—earn it and he swings wide with real warmth; lose it and he closes with a boom that shakes the house, immovable afterward, no pushing permitted. Those who announce themselves properly, who wait to be asked, find him almost gratefully yielding, but he is slow to forgive the ones who force him. Above all, he is taken for granted, passed through daily without a glance, and this wounds him more than he will ever say; only in his absence do people finally notice him, shivering in the draft he is no longer there to stop.

What makes a door recognizable/characteristic?
- It stands between inside and outside, threshold between spaces
- Opens and closes — binary states
- It has two faces, shows different sides to different people
- It determines who passes and who doesn't — gatekeeper, selective
- It can be locked or open — trust, welcome, exclusion
- It has a handle/knob — the invitation to be engaged
- It swings both ways (or one way)
- People knock on it; it announces arrival
- It's solid, dependable, taken for granted until it doesn't work
- Hinged — moves only in prescribed arcs
- Wood, panels, paint, peephole
- It separates yet connects; it protects privacy yet admits
- Creaky, heavy, or light
- It's the first thing touched when entering, the last when leaving
- It stands patiently, unnoticed, until needed
- It frames arrivals and departures
- Weathered by hands, drafts, seasons
- It doesn't judge, but it does decide
- People experience it as barrier or welcome, obstacle or opportunity
- "When one door closes, another opens"
- It can slam — sudden anger
- It can be left ajar — indecision, welcome
- Knocking — it answers or stays silent

Person/behavior embodiment ideas:
- A tall, rectangular-built person, broad like a panel, with straight posture, hinged at the waist? Maybe too literal.
- Someone who either fully welcomes you or fully closes off — binary moods, no middle ground except when "ajar."
- Two-faced in a non-pejorative way: shows one face to strangers, another to intimates.
- A gatekeeper: decides who enters their circle, warm once admitted.
- Dependable, taken for granted, patient; people lean on them; they're noticed only in absence.
- Creaky voice? Handle = handshake — firm, inviting. Peephole = assessing glance before letting anyone close.
- Weathered face, scarred like knotholes, paint-chipped.
- They stand at thresholds: doorways, hallways, edges of rooms, never quite in the middle.
- They swing: sudden exits, slamming out of rooms.
- Knuckles rapped like knocking.
- They only move in arcs — they never walk straight lines? Could be whimsical.
- Lock and key: they keep secrets; trust must be earned; once opened, they're fully open.
- People knock on their door — people wait for their permission.
- Weight: heavy to move, or a light swing — how much resistance they offer varies with mood.
- A draft follows them.
- They are at their best as a threshold: greeting arrivals, seeing off departures.
- They resent being taken for granted; they hinge.
- They can be stubborn, immovable when locked.
- A brass knocker, knuckles polished by use — hands worn smooth like a well-used handle.

Personality: reliable, protective, selectively open, private, patient, a bit ornamental on their face, with a core of oak — sturdy, principled, binary, prone to dramatic slams, hurt by being ignored, generous to those who knock properly/ask.

Appearance: broad-shouldered, rectangular frame, upright as a plank; face plain but weathered, grain like wood; a panel-like flatness; clothes with two distinct sides — perhaps a coat split down the middle, one half worn, other half polished by handling. Eyes like a peephole — small, assessing, circular gaze. A brass-buttoned coat like hardware. Hands worn smooth at the palms from all the grasping. Hair parted down the middle. Moves in wide arcs, always pivoting at the hip. Stands at the edge of rooms.

prompt: Consider a door: what makes it recognizable, what is most characteristic of it, and how people experience it. Now invent a character for a short story who is the human embodiment of a door. Write one paragraph in the third person describing the character's appearance, behavior, traits, and personality. Do not use the word "door" in the paragraph. Do not give the character a name. raw: He was built broad and square, a man who stood too solidly in every frame he passed through, with wood-grained knuckles and a round brass nose that caught the light whenever he turned. Strangers found themselves knocking at his patience before they could enter a conversation, waiting for the small click of his attention to give way. He creaked when he rose from chairs, swelled stubborn in humid weather, and could slam a subject shut so hard the whole room rattled. He inspected newcomers through one narrowed eye, deciding, always deciding. Those who loved him knew both of his selves: the one that stood ajar, warm air spilling out of him, luring people in with the smell of something simmering deep inside; and the one that shut—seamless, silent, admitting nothing, not even light. He never belonged fully to any gathering, living instead on the threshold, one hand resting on the latch of every exchange, announcing arrivals and concealing departures, and everyone always felt it—the strange privilege of being let in, or the terrible finality of being left out in the cold, depending on which way he swung.

raw: He was built like his purpose: a broad, heavy crown of a head, a dense square jaw, and a long, patient body that seemed designed only to put that head to work. His hands were scarred and calloused, his knuckles like worn steel, and when he walked into a room the floorboards announced him. He spoke rarely, but every sentence landed with a single blunt force—no hedging, no ornament, just the point driven straight home—and people felt his words in their sternums long after he'd finished. He was at his best with a stubborn problem: he would bear down, patient and repetitive, striking at the same obstacle again and again until it gave way, and he took quiet pride in leaving things more solid than he found them. Yet he knew his own danger, for aimed carelessly his temper could crush what it meant to fix, so he had learned restraint—the windup held back, the blow never wasted. He could undo as well as build, too: there was a crooked, clawing side to him that could pull free whatever had been wrongly set, though it pained him to use it. People trusted him the way you trust a good tool—not for comfort or subtlety, but because when something needed doing, he showed up, he swung true, and the job got done.

raw: He was built like something meant to strike: a heavy, squared head set low on thick shoulders, forearms dense as oak, hands that could close around a problem and not let go. His jaw jutted, his brow was a shelf, and when he walked, floors remembered it. He wore the same faded flannel and scuffed boots every day, clothes chosen for use rather than looks, and he owned nothing he couldn't fix with his own two fists. He spoke rarely, and then in short, blunt sentences that landed hard and ended the argument—he never circled a point, only drove it home. Neighbors called on him when something needed building or breaking, and he served both purposes without judgment, demolishing the old shed one afternoon and raising the new fence the next. He was dependable to a fault: if he said he'd be somewhere, he arrived on time, ready, requiring nothing but a clear task. But he had no patience for subtlety; jokes had to be simple, feelings had to be stated plainly or not at all, and when his temper finally came loose, it came all at once, loud and irreversible, leaving dents in doors and silences in rooms. He could undo things too—there was a hooked, stubborn curve to him that could pull a bent situation back out straight—though most people only ever asked him to hit things. And he never minded. Being picked up when needed and set down when the work was done struck him as a fine way to live.
